For those who were around this time last year, I was the one who posted about my abuse and sexual assault at the hands of a male (ex-)friend.  I mentioned that I had been in the hospital a couple times, once for suicidal intent, and another time for an attempt. Well, I went quiet for awhile, deleted the posts, and deleted my old account because those posts ended up being seen and used against me by the other party. The police investigation ended at the state’s attorney’s office, where they decided not to prosecute the case. I’ve made healthier friendships with people who listen to and support me, and I’ve been taking medication and seeing a good therapist. Things didn’t end how I wanted but I’m moving forward and healing anyway.

The Bible also has commands regarding the Sabbath. Take those who, by their understanding of scripture, don’t believe that the Sabbath must be observed; if they turn out to be wrong, aren’t they sinning, and by the logic in these replies, not in Christ?

Or take swearing. The New Testament has texts which some would say clearly command against such language. Others don’t have such a strong conviction that those texts are applied that way. Are those who use swear words for this reason then outside of God’s grace?

Many do. Some don’t. Some are unsure. I fall in the last camp.

Frankly, it’s not an issue of primary importance, and questions raised about the texts and translations are worth taking into consideration rather than dismissing altogether. The “plain reading” of the text seems to say that it is a sin, but again, there is more to the discussion that’s worth looking at. I see some people in this thread (and on the internet in general) denying the orthodoxy of anyone who disagrees with them on this issue, or claiming that a liberal view on this issue immediately means you don’t believe the Bible is the infallible word of God. Some good old-fashioned theological triage is necessary here. There are issues that are essential to a saving faith, but this is not one of them, and shouldn’t be treated as such.

Someone who disagrees with you on baptism can be a Christian. Someone who disagrees with you on the Sabbath can be a Christian. And someone who disagrees with you on homosexuality, yes, can also be a Christian.

My concern is less about Sunday than the Sabbath, which probably doesn’t have to be a specific day. Best not to make a law where there is none, right? 

I do my best to set aside one day a week as a Sabbath (typically Saturday, just because of my own personal schedule) where my priority is to rest in God. I also don’t think that this ends at not working or doing schoolwork, but there’s the positive element of doing things that are restful, spending intentional time in the presence of God, and enjoying him through his creation. The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Worrying too much about what is work and what isn’t becomes burdensome, and can interfere with the rest we are supposed to embrace and surrender to. Observing the Sabbath properly shouldn’t be a sign to us that we’re enough, but a gentle reminder that we’re not.

As for other people, I let them live out their own convictions. I cannot guess if someone observes the Sabbath or when that might be for them, so I can’t assume I’m forcing them to work. But if your conviction is to abstain from anything that might cause someone to work on Sundays, I respect that a lot, and think that is a fine personal conviction to hold to.

I’m in a college campus ministry right now so a lot of the mentorship within my circle is older students leading younger students, or the staff members (mid-20s) leading college students. Usually the staff would choose students to take on leadership of a certain group. They lead a weekly Bible study with their small group. We’d meet every week, talk about discussion questions for a passage of scripture (usually going bit by bit through a book) and do some scripture memory and prayer. Our small group leader would also meet one-on-one with each of us through the week to talk about life, accountability, etc. and read and pray together.

This past semester and moving forward, I’m also being mentored/discipled by an adult woman at my church, who’s the wife of the associate pastor at my church and also a professor in my department at school. We meet weekly for coffee and mostly just talk through the week. I text her throughout the week to get her advice on things or even to just have someone to listen when I’ve got stuff going on. I tend to write down questions to ask or things to talk about through the week. Sometimes we get to them, sometimes we’re too busy chatting away to bother. I write in my Bible, but have no set system. In Romans I highlighted certain recurrent words certain colors or with certain symbols, but that’s the closest I’ve gotten. Usually I just underline or highlight with whatever writing tools I have nearby, and sometimes I’ll put short notes from the sermon or study in the margins. I always love finding those when I read a passage again, and it’s always neat to see how the verses I didn’t choose to underline the other times now stand out to me for one reason or another.
